step1_summary: Chief complaint: Persistent dry cough and runny nose for ~5–6 days.

Symptoms: Dry, persistent cough (keeps patient up at night), runny nose; mild sore throat from coughing; chills/shivers (especially at night); one episode of self-limited diarrhea at onset; generalized muscle aches (especially arms/legs), lethargy/weakness; no chest pain, no breathlessness at rest, no nausea/vomiting, no rash.
Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes, hypertension (both reportedly well-controlled).
Medications/allergies: Metformin (diabetes), Lisinopril (hypertension); no medication allergies.

Family/social history: Father with type 2 diabetes, lives with partner (who is well), works in IT (mostly sedentary), ex-smoker (quit 6 months ago), drinks wine (2–3 glasses, ~3x/week), no recreational drug use mentioned.
Vital signs/exam findings: Not provided in transcript.

V: Pulmonary embolism: Dry cough, mild dyspnea on exertion could suggest this, but absence of chest pain or real breathlessness is against.
I: Viral upper respiratory tract infection (e.g., rhinovirus, influenza, RSV, COVID-19): Subacute onset, constitutional symptoms (chills, myalgias, lethargy), runny nose, dry cough, self-limited GI symptoms all fit.
Atypical pneumonia (e.g., Mycoplasma, Chlamydia): Dry cough, systemic symptoms, prolonged course. However, lack of fever measurement, and less common in age/setting.
Acute bronchitis: Subacute dry cough after preceding URTI, constitutional symptoms.
N: Lung cancer: Ex-smoker, cough, but time course (days) and associated viral/constitutional symptoms make this much less likely.
D: ACE inhibitor–induced cough: On lisinopril, persistent dry cough possible side effect. However, recent onset, associated runny nose, chills, and myalgias argue for an acute process.
C: Allergic rhinitis: Runny nose, cough, but acute systemic symptoms and myalgias, not typical.
A: Influenza or COVID-19: As above under infections, autoimmune less likely.
E: Poor diabetes control predisposing to infection: Her DM is described as controlled, but may increase infection risk.
Electrolyte disturbance (post-diarrhea): Diarrhea was brief and resolved; not enough ongoing symptoms.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Acute viral upper respiratory tract infection (including influenza, RSV, COVID-19)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Symptoms developed subacutely with clear systemic features (chills, myalgias, lethargy) and respiratory involvement (dry, persistent cough, runny nose) suggest a viral syndrome. Recent onset, duration <1 week, gradual improvement, and self-limited GI involvement fit common viral illnesses.
supporting_evidence: Dry cough, runny nose, mild sore throat, chills
Self-limited diarrhea at onset (can occur in some viruses)
No significant chest pain or breathlessness; partner is asymptomatic

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Viral bronchitis may present after/with URI; persistent dry cough with systemic symptoms. Lack of significant chest findings or productive sputum points away from bacterial bronchitis/pneumonia.
opposing_evidence: No chest pain, no increased breathlessness, no sputum production

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Atypical pathogens (e.g., Mycoplasma) can cause dry cough with systemic symptoms, but patient lacks significant fever, dyspnea or chest findings; no epidemiologic risk factors given.
opposing_evidence: No breathlessness, no chest pain, no fever measured, mild illness course

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Lisinopril is a known cause of chronic dry cough, but the temporal association with acute systemic symptoms, recent onset, and runny nose suggest new infection rather than drug effect.
opposing_evidence: New onset only in last week, not temporally linked to starting medication
Systemic symptoms not typical for ACE inhibitor cough
